summary: Hermann Bonitz worked in philosophy and other fields. He studied at the University of Leipzig (~1830–1834) and Humboldt University of Berlin under Friedrich Adolf Trendelenburg (~1834–1836), later holding posts at the University of Vienna (~1849–1867) and the Prussian Ministry (~1867–1888).

A scholar of Indology and linguistics, Brockhaus studied at Leipzig, Göttingen, and Bonn under August Wilhelm von Schlegel and Christian Lassen. He served as professor at the University of Jena (1839–1841) and the University of Leipzig (from 1841 until 1877).

Hermann Brunnhofer worked in Indology and linguistics. He studied at Bonn, Berlin under Albrecht Weber, and Zurich (Ph.D. 1871). His posts included librarian at Aargauer Kantonsbibliothek (1873–1888), translator at Saint Petersburg State University (1891–1901), and Dozent at Bern (1901–1914).

A scholar in Indology and linguistics, Hermann Camillo Kellner studied at the University of Leipzig under Hermann Brockhaus and Georg Curtius (Ph.D. 1859–1862). He taught at Thomasschule zu Leipzig (~1864–1900) and Gymnasium Zwickau (1887).

Working in linguistics and Indology, Collitz earned his Ph.D. at Göttingen under August Fick and completed his Habilitation at Halle. He taught at Halle (1885), Bryn Mawr College (1885–1907), and held a chair at Johns Hopkins University (1907–1928).

Hermann Diels worked in philosophy, history/archaeology, and other fields. He studied at Humboldt University of Berlin (~1866–1867) and the University of Bonn under Hermann Usener (~1867–1870), later holding a post at Humboldt University of Berlin (~1882–1921).
Hermann Ernst Grassmann studied at Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg (~1888–1893) and held a professorship at the University of Giessen (~1904–1922).

Ethé specialized in Indology and Iranian/Central Asian studies. He studied at Greifswald, Leipzig (Ph.D.), Munich (PD), and Oxford. He catalogued manuscripts at the Bodleian Library (1872) and became Professor of Oriental Languages at Aberystwyth University in 1875.

A scholar in Indology and linguistics, Mögling studied at the University of Tübingen (~1830–1834) and Basel Mission Seminary (1834). He served as a teacher and preacher for the Basel Mission from 1838 to 1852.

Hermann Fränkel studied at Berlin under Ulrich von Wilamowitz-Moellendorff, Bonn, and Göttingen (~1910–1915). He held academic posts at the University of Göttingen (~1920–1935) and Stanford University (~1935–1953).

An Indology and history/archaeology scholar, Goetz earned his Ph.D. at Munich and studied under Jean Philippe Vogel. He worked at the Kern Institute, Baroda Museum (1939–1953), National Gallery of Modern Art (1953–1955), and Heidelberg University (1961–1976).

Grassmann worked in Indology, linguistics, and other fields after studying at Humboldt University of Berlin under Schleiermacher and Boeckh (1827–1830). He taught at several schools, notably the Friedrich-Wilhelms-Schule Stettin (1843–1852) and the Marienstiftsgymnasium as professor (~1844–1877).

A specialist in Indology and linguistics, Gundert earned his Ph.D. from the University of Tübingen (~1831–1835). He held posts at the Church Missionary Society (~1836–1838), the Basel Mission (from 1838), and headed Calwer Verlag from 1860.

Güntert worked in linguistics, Indology, and religious studies. He studied at Heidelberg under Hermann Osthoff and Christian Bartholomae (Ph.D. 1908). He served as professor at the University of Rostock (1921) and Heidelberg University (PD 1913, ordinary professor 1926–1945).

A scholar in linguistics and Indology, Hirt studied at Freiburg and Leipzig under Brugmann, Leskien, Zarncke, Sievers, and Windisch (Ph.D., Habilitation). He was a PD at Leipzig (1891–1912) and ord. Professor at Giessen (1912–1936).

Hermann Hunger, active in history/archaeology and linguistics, studied at Vienna, Heidelberg, and Münster. He held posts at the German Archaeological Institute (~1968–1970) and the University of Chicago (~1970–1973), and served as professor at the University of Vienna (1978–2007).

Hermann Hupfeld worked in religious studies and linguistics. He studied at the University of Marburg (~1813–1817) and Halle-Wittenberg (~1822–1824), later holding posts at Marburg (~1825–1843) and Halle-Wittenberg (~1843–1866).

A scholar in Indology, linguistics, and Buddhist studies, Jacobi studied at Berlin and Bonn under Johann Gildemeister. He served as professor at the University of Münster (1876–1885) and the University of Bonn (PD 1875, professor 1889–1922).

A scholar of Buddhist studies and Indology, Kopp studied at Leipzig, Heidelberg, and Walleser-Institut under Max Walleser and Heinrich Zimmer. He served on the Pali Text Society board (1936–1953) and directed the Walleser-Institut (1954–1958) and Mainz Academy (1959–1964).

A scholar of Indology, Hermann Kreyenborg studied at Humboldt University of Berlin and the University of Münster (1910–1921, Ph.D. supervised by Richard Schmidt). He served as a librarian at the University and State Library of Münster from 1922 to 1954.
